A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with readable main text, figures, equations, references, and appendices. The retained material can be matched across restructuring and figure renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments across 135 chaotic systems, including model comparisons, attractor reconstruction, and context-length analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds context-shuffling, nonstationarity, initial-condition, and measured double-pendulum forecasting results.

M1.justification: The same five pretrained Chronos variants perform channel-independent zero-shot forecasting. Added diagnostic experiments and expanded fine-tuning comparisons do not change this forecasting procedure; proposed architectural adaptations remain future work.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained simulated dynamical systems, v2 adds measured double-pendulum data with experimental noise and dissipation (Appendix D) and systematically damped, nonstationary trajectories across the 135 systems (Appendix E). These substantially extend coverage to real measurements and distribution shift.

E2.justification: NBEATS, TiDE, NVAR, Transformer, LSTM, and the constant-forecast baseline remain. Appendix F.2 adds an explicit qualitative comparison of fine-tuned Chronos-base against zero-shot forecasts, expanding v1's brief preliminary fine-tuning remarks.

E3.justification: The principal 512-point context, 300-point test, and 135-system benchmark design remains. New protocols include shuffling context blocks while preserving the final block, a 200-trajectory initial-condition probe, pendulum preprocessing and evaluation windows, and exponential-damping sweeps. These are substantial additions to evaluation design.

E4.justification: Sections 5.3–5.4 and Appendices C–F add context-overlap comparisons, shuffled-context ablations, attractor-density analysis, and nonstationarity robustness tests, while expanding fine-tuning diagnostics. Earlier multivariate, context-length, attractor-metric, and model-size analyses remain.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 5 describes standard deviations; corresponding v2 Figure 6 specifies medians and standard errors. v2 also adds a matched t-test for context overlap. Figure 2 drops v1's disclosure of averaging 20 independent stochastic forecasts, without establishing that the actual run count changed.

E6.justification: New findings include benefits from shuffled long contexts, declining VPT with nonstationarity, and an initial-density/VPT correlation of 0.26 ± 0.03 across 2700 cases, plus pendulum and fine-tuning outcomes. Figure 3's VPT distributions and the context-length VPT curves also change. Changed aggregation reporting prevents interpreting these revisions as straightforward performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds a mathematical definition of exponential trajectory modulation and parameterizes nonstationarity through its damping strength, including stationary and damped limits. Existing Lorenz equations and forecasting-metric definitions remain equivalent; no new theorem or proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract newly identifies context parroting as a mechanism for capturing chaotic dynamics and attributes success to in-context learning. This elevates a mechanistic explanation into a central contribution beyond v1's comparative forecasting and attractor-reconstruction claims, although the four enumerated contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops the interpretation around motif matching and learning the attractor's natural measure. It adds limitations involving rare states and nonstationarity, interprets unsuccessful fine-tuning through task shift, and discusses possible adaptations. These extend v1's emphasis on generic features, dimensional lifting, and hypothesized in-context learning.

D1.justification: Appendix F.1 supplies implementation sources, architecture settings, and lookback search grids for all five trained baselines. Additional details cover pendulum coordinate conversion and downsampling, and fine-tuning data and scripts. These substantially improve documentation without establishing changes to previously used settings; code and data access statements remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the measured dataset, Darts implementations, fine-tuning limitations, low-rank adaptation, and proposed robustness improvements. Section 2 also adds Ekambaram et al. on time-series foundation models. The broader related-work framing and first-large-scale-evaluation positioning remain.

P1.justification: Most existing exposition is retained. Targeted edits revise the abstract and conclusion, replace numbered methods subsections with run-in headings, separate existing result discussions into focused subsections, and relocate the sMAPE explanation to Appendix B.2.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns Figure 2, expands the initial-condition illustration into paired Figure 8, and adds several mechanism and robustness figures. The former two-panel context-length figure becomes three-panel Figure 6 with a shuffling experiment. Plot axes, sizing, captions, and placement also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the previously conjectural mechanism account with targeted context-matching and shuffling tests, examines real measurements and distribution-shift limits, and supplies missing baseline hyperparameters. These improve evidential depth and reproducibility. Unexplained VPT revisions and the pendulum experiment's seven-versus-eight-window inconsistency remain reporting weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.
